claims.text: A machine-learning surrogate model can predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting for refractory alloys.
The surrogate model can achieve reasonable accuracy while costing substantially less than fully ab initio free-energy calculations.
The target materials are multicomponent refractory alloys, including high-entropy alloys, for which only partial experimental characterization or limited ab initio data may be available.
Physically guided descriptors such as atomic-size mismatch, mixing enthalpy, and elastic parameters can be used to train the melting-property surrogate.
Accurate melting data from ab initio free-energy calculations or experiments can serve as training data for the surrogate.
The trained surrogate can screen untested alloy compositions in a high-throughput manner.
Reliable surrogate training requires a representative dataset spanning the relevant compositions and temperatures.
Targeted ab initio calculations or experimental measurements can be used to validate the surrogate's accuracy.
Atomic-radius mismatch, mixing enthalpy, and electronic-structure parameters capture local atomic structure and chemical surroundings relevant to melting.
A data-driven model can learn the fundamental thermodynamic relationships represented by ab initio calculations.
The surrogate avoids the computational scaling cost of molecular-dynamics-based thermodynamic integration.

Predictions of melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting will agree with measurements or high-fidelity ab initio results to within 10–20% relative error.
The surrogate predictions will be obtained at a fraction of the computational cost of the standard ab initio free-energy approach.
The standard ab initio free-energy approach using thermodynamic integration is highly accurate but prohibitively expensive for large-scale screening.
The surrogate becomes less reliable for compositions or temperatures substantially outside its training domain.
The quality of the training data limits the model's ultimate predictive performance.
Complex phase behavior absent from the training data can limit transferability to new refractory-alloy chemistries.
Comparing predictions against targeted measurements for multiple previously unseen compositions can test the model.
Statistically significant deviations from predicted ranges across multiple new compositions would falsify or require refinement of the hypothesis.
